stem: In PostgreSQL, row security is enabled on a table with `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` but the table has no policy. What can an ordinary user do with its rows?
key: See and modify no rows, because a default-deny policy is used
distractors: See and modify all rows, because the SQL privilege system alone decides access
See all rows but update none of them
Nothing, because every query fails with an error until a policy is created
explanation: With row security enabled and no policy, a default-deny policy is used, so no rows are visible or can be modified. Seeing and modifying all rows is wrong because all normal access must be allowed by a row security policy. Seeing all rows is wrong because no rows will be visible or updatable. Failing with an error is wrong because typically no error occurs when a row is not visible.
extract: If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used, meaning that no rows are visible or can be modified.

stem: In PostgreSQL, an `UPDATE` policy defines only a `USING` expression and no `WITH CHECK` expression. Against what are the new rows produced by an `UPDATE` checked?
distractors: Against no expression, so any new row value is allowed
Against an implicit `WITH CHECK (true)` expression
Against the `USING` expressions of the `SELECT` policies only
explanation: When no `WITH CHECK` expression is defined, the `USING` expression is used both for the visible rows and for the new rows allowed to be added. Checking against no expression, against an implicit `WITH CHECK (true)` expression, and against the `SELECT` policies only are three other choices than the `USING` expression of the policy itself.
extract: For policies that can have both USING and WITH CHECK expressions (ALL and UPDATE), if no WITH CHECK expression is defined, then the USING expression will be used both to determine which rows are visible (normal USING case) and which new rows will be allowed to be added (WITH CHECK case).

stem: In PostgreSQL, two permissive policies and one restrictive policy of the same command type apply to a query. How are their expressions combined?
key: The permissive expressions are combined with OR, the restrictive one with AND, and the results with AND
distractors: All three expressions are combined with OR, so any one of them grants access
All three expressions are combined with AND, so every policy must pass
Only the restrictive policy is applied, because the stricter policy overrides the others
explanation: Permissive expressions are combined with OR, restrictive expressions with AND, and the two results with AND. Combining all three with OR is wrong because restrictive policies are combined using AND. Combining all three with AND is wrong because at least one permissive policy must grant access, so permissive policies are not all required. Applying only the restrictive policy is wrong because without a permissive policy access is denied.
extract: Thus all the PERMISSIVE policy expressions are combined using OR, all the RESTRICTIVE policy expressions are combined using AND, and the results are combined using AND.

stem: In PostgreSQL, how can the owner of a table be made subject to the row security policies of its own table?
key: With `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`
distractors: With `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, which applies to every role including the owner
By granting the owner the `BYPASSRLS` attribute
It is not possible, because table owners always bypass row security
explanation: A table owner can choose to be subject to row security with `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. Enabling row security is wrong because the table owner is typically not subject to the policies. Granting `BYPASSRLS` is wrong because roles with that attribute always bypass row security. Saying it is impossible is wrong because the owner can choose to be subject to row security.
extract: though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

stem: In PostgreSQL 15 and later, which schema usage pattern does the default configuration support without any change to its privileges or search path?
key: Constraining ordinary users to user-private schemas
distractors: Keeping the default search path and granting privileges to create in the public schema
Removing the public schema from the default search path
Installing the shared applications into the private schema of each user
explanation: The default configuration of PostgreSQL 15 and later supports constraining ordinary users to user-private schemas. Keeping the default search path with create privileges on the public schema is the default only in databases upgraded from PostgreSQL 14 or earlier. Removing the public schema from the search path needs a change to `postgresql.conf` or `ALTER ROLE ALL SET search_path`. Installing shared applications in private schemas is wrong because they go into separate schemas.
extract: In PostgreSQL 15 and later, the default configuration supports this usage pattern.

stem: In Kafka, a connection matches the quota of its (user, client-id) group, the quota of its user and the quota of its client-id. Which quota is applied to the connection?
key: The most specific quota matching the connection
distractors: The smallest of the matching quotas
The sum of the matching quotas
The client-id quota, whatever other quotas match
explanation: Kafka applies the most specific quota matching the connection. The smallest of the matching quotas, the sum of the matching quotas, and the client-id quota whatever else matches are three other rules than the one the documentation states.
extract: For a given connection, the most specific quota matching the connection is applied.

stem: According to the Kafka design documentation, on what basis is the fixed quota that each unique client group receives by default defined?
distractors: Per cluster, as one fixed bandwidth for each client
Per topic, so that each topic has its own quota for each client
Per partition, so that each partition leader enforces its own quota
explanation: The quota is defined on a per-broker basis. A fixed quota per cluster is wrong because Kafka decided that per broker is much better than a cluster wide bandwidth per client. A quota per topic is wrong because quotas apply to (user, client-id), user or client-id groups. A quota per partition is wrong because brokers enforce quotas for each group of clients sharing a quota.
extract: This quota is defined on a per-broker basis.

stem: In Java 25, the snippet works out what a Kafka client group can use with a per-broker quota of 10 MB/s, 3 brokers and 4 producer instances sharing the quota evenly. What does it print?
key:
per-broker quota MB/s: 10.0
cluster-wide ceiling MB/s: 30.0
share per producer instance at the ceiling MB/s: 7.5
share per producer instance on one broker MB/s: 2.5
distractors:
per-broker quota MB/s: 10.0
cluster-wide ceiling MB/s: 10.0
share per producer instance at the ceiling MB/s: 2.5
share per producer instance on one broker MB/s: 0.8

per-broker quota MB/s: 10.0
cluster-wide ceiling MB/s: 30.0
share per producer instance at the ceiling MB/s: 120.0
share per producer instance on one broker MB/s: 40.0

per-broker quota MB/s: 10.0
cluster-wide ceiling MB/s: 3.3
share per producer instance at the ceiling MB/s: 0.8
share per producer instance on one broker MB/s: 2.5
explanation: The quota applies per broker, so the ceiling is 10 MB/s times 3 brokers, and 4 instances share it evenly, which gives the recorded output. The output with a ceiling of 10.0 is wrong because the quota is defined per broker, not for the cluster. The output with 120.0 is wrong because the ceiling is divided among the instances, not multiplied by them. The output with a ceiling of 3.3 is wrong because the quota is multiplied by the number of brokers, not divided.
extract: This quota is defined on a per-broker basis.

stem: In Resilience4j, which statement about the `SemaphoreBulkhead`, one of the two bulkhead implementations that limit the number of concurrent executions, is correct?
key: It is up to the client to size the thread pool consistently with the bulkhead configuration
distractors: It limits concurrency with a bounded queue and a fixed thread pool
It provides a shadow thread pool for each bulkhead, as Hystrix does
It sizes the thread pool automatically from the bulkhead configuration
explanation: With the `SemaphoreBulkhead` it is up to the client to size the thread pool consistently with the bulkhead configuration. The bounded queue and fixed thread pool belong to the `FixedThreadPoolBulkhead`. A shadow thread pool is wrong because, unlike Hystrix, it does not provide a shadow thread pool option. Automatic sizing is wrong because the client is responsible for the sizing.

stem: In Kubernetes on Linux nodes, how is a `cpu` limit enforced when a container approaches it?
key: By CPU throttling, with the kernel restricting access to the CPU
distractors: By terminating the container with an out of memory (OOM) kill
Loosely, since a container may use more CPU than its limit when the node has spare CPU
By the scheduler, which refuses to place Pods whose containers could exceed the limit
explanation: A cpu limit is enforced by CPU throttling, where the kernel restricts access to the CPU. The OOM kill is wrong because it enforces memory limits. Loose enforcement is wrong because containers may not use more CPU than their cpu limit. The scheduler is wrong because the kubelet and container runtime apply the limits and the kernel enforces them.
extract: cpu limits are enforced by CPU throttling.

stem: In Kubernetes, when a Node runs out of resources, in which order are Pods evicted by quality of service class?
distractors: `Guaranteed` first, then `Burstable`, and finally `BestEffort` Pods
`Burstable` first, then `BestEffort`, and finally `Guaranteed` Pods
`Burstable` first, then `Guaranteed`, and finally `BestEffort` Pods
explanation: Kubernetes first evicts `BestEffort` Pods, followed by `Burstable` and finally `Guaranteed` Pods. The order starting with `Guaranteed`, the order starting with `Burstable` then `BestEffort`, and the order starting with `Burstable` then `Guaranteed` are three other orders than the single one the documentation gives.
extract: When a Node runs out of resources, Kubernetes will first evict BestEffort Pods running on that Node, followed by Burstable and finally Guaranteed Pods.

stem: In Kubernetes on Linux nodes, what can happen to a container that uses more memory than its `memory` limit?
key: The kernel may terminate it with an out of memory (OOM) kill
distractors: It is slowed down by CPU throttling until its memory use falls
It is killed immediately, at the moment it goes over the limit
It is never terminated, because the limit only affects scheduling
explanation: A container that uses more than its memory limit may be terminated by the kernel. CPU throttling is wrong because it enforces cpu limits. An immediate kill is wrong because a container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. Never terminating is wrong because memory limits are enforced by the kernel with OOM kills.
extract: When a container uses more than its memory limit, the kernel may terminate it.
